demonstrations.title: How pitch coordination changes
demonstrations.mechanism: The cricothyroid muscle links two laryngeal cartilages: thyroid and cricoid. Their relative motion can separate the vocal-fold attachments and lengthen the folds. Pitch reflects coordinated stiffness, length, effective vibrating mass and pressure, with several muscles involved.

cues.text: On an easy “oo,” glide a little higher and back without getting louder.
cues.notice: Notice whether the pitch moves easily. A small glide is enough.

cues.text: Sing an easy “oo,” then a nearby higher note at a comfortable level.
cues.notice: Compare the pitch and effort; do not reach for the top of your range.

demonstrations.title: The mouth–nose connection
demonstrations.mechanism: The velum, or soft palate, helps control the opening to the nasal pathway. Raising it can reduce nasal coupling, changing resonances and cancellations in the sound.

cues.text: Gently sustain “ng” as in “sing,” then release to an easy “ah.”
cues.notice: Listen for a change in sound and notice the tongue release. Several structures change together.

cues.text: Repeat one comfortable “ng–ah” and compare it with your previous attempt.
cues.notice: Notice the difference without trying to force a particular palate position.

demonstrations.title: Vowel shape and tone
demonstrations.mechanism: Tongue and jaw positions change tract constrictions. These alter which frequencies are reinforced, contributing to vowel differences.

cues.text: On an easy “ah,” allow a small jaw release while keeping the note comfortable.
cues.notice: Listen for a tone change; keep pitch and level similar if you can.

cues.text: At an easy pitch, alternate a gentle “ee” and “ah.”
cues.notice: Compare vowel colour. Your tongue, lips and jaw may all move.

demonstrations.title: Pitch and tone are different controls
demonstrations.mechanism: Vocal-fold vibration supplies excitation. The vocal tract filters that sound, emphasizing some frequency regions. In a simplified model, source repetition sets the fundamental frequency and tract shape affects the spectral envelope.

cues.text: Keep an easy note while gently changing “oo” toward “ah.”
cues.notice: Listen for tone colour changing even if the note stays similar.

cues.text: Keep an easy “oo” and try a small pitch glide.
cues.notice: Compare a pitch change with the vowel change; neither trial isolates every structure.
